Apple must respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with Brazil's antitrust regulator, alleging that Apple is interpreting its obligations under a recent local App Store antitrust agreement in a restrictive manner. Details below.

Background

Two months ago, Apple announced that it now allows developers to distribute apps in Brazil via alternative app marketplaces.

The change was part of a settlement resolving a years-long antitrust investigation, which stemmed from a complaint filed by Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods other than Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "Core Technology Fee" on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside of the App Store. You can read more about the structure here.

Epic challenges Apple's implementation

According to a report today by Brazilian newspaper O Globo (republished by MacMagazine), Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE, accusing Apple of creating "structural, technical, and channel access barriers" that undermine the real-world viability of alternative app distribution.

Epic noted that, while the new terms in Brazil apply only to iOS apps, Apple's agreement with CADE "clearly covers iPadOS."

The company is also reportedly objecting to so-called "scare screens," which it says deter users from installing apps outside the App Store, as well as to the current installation flow, which Epic says requires nine steps — three more than Apple's current implementation in Europe.

O Globo reports that Epic added that Apple's initial installation flow in Europe required 15 steps, but after the company was asked to streamline it down to six, "download abandonment dropped from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "far exceed what is necessary to calculate fees" and said this allows the company "to monitor competitors' business models."

CADE has given Apple until Monday to submit a response, according to O Globo. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter.
